html:
Gateway admission, authentication and transport flows

The controller selects and authorizes an operation. A Gateway performs it on the selected host. These diagrams follow the intervening availability, identity and delivery checks. They complement Gateway architecture and Gateway state and recovery. A successful connection is neither operation permission nor a completion receipt.

Owners and data boundaries

flowchart TD Run[Accepted run and captured Gateway IDs] --> Admission[Activity availability and resource admission] Registry[Controller registry: endpoint, node, pin and health] --> Admission Admission --> Client[Selected Gateway client] Permission[Live operation permission and exact consent] --> Client Client --> HTTP[Pinned HTTPS and signed request] Client --> WSS[Authenticated outbound session] ControllerKey[Retained controller identity] --> HTTP ControllerKey --> WSS HTTP --> Middleware[Gateway authentication middleware] WSS --> Dispatcher[Gateway outbound dispatcher] Pairing[Gateway pairing revision and replay fences] --> Middleware Pairing --> Dispatcher Middleware --> Policy[Runtime epoch, admission and request policy] Dispatcher --> Policy Policy --> Service[GatewayService and typed provider] Service --> Effect[Host operation and its actual receipt] Effect --> Evidence[Controller operation evidence and reconciliation] Evidence --> View[Progress, trace and result presentation]

Controller registrations, live sockets and Gateway jobs have different owners. The live session registry contains pending futures and observation queues; it is not durable execution history. Gateway pairing binds a controller identity, while request context carries that identity and its pairing revision into dispatch. The Gateway's retained runtime state and safety fences are described in publication and authority.

Boundary Implementation
Offline Activity admission gateway_admission.py, called by resource_scheduler.py
Inbound controller authentication gateway_auth.py, client_auth.py, auth_middleware.py
Gateway pairing and request provenance pairing.py, authorization.py
Outbound TLS and mutual proof outbound_tls.py, Gateway proof, controller proof
Outbound requests and responses controller session, Gateway dispatcher, connection route

Availability before an execution slot

The scheduler starts this probe when its selected-target availability signal is false, or when that target already has a pending probe. It does not perform an extra network round trip before every operation on a connected target.

sequenceDiagram participant A as Activity scheduler participant P as Per-run probe state participant H as Registry health worker participant S as Capacity and resource scheduler A->>S: Enqueue accepted target and resource claims A->>P: Check unavailable target P->>H: Start one daemon health check with five-second deadline P-->>A: Pending Note over A,S: No execution slot is acquired while probing opt Health worker finishes H-->>P: Result and monotonic completion time end A->>P: Poll result or deadline alt Connected before deadline P-->>A: True and discard successful probe entry A->>S: Refresh availability and attempt ordinary admission else Unavailable, disabled, missing or deadline exceeded P-->>A: False retained for this run and target A->>S: Release queue reservation A->>A: Save pre-dispatch rejection through the Activity owner Note over A,H: A late success cannot redispatch the rejected operation end

The deadline covers discovery and authentication as well as the health request. The worker does not hold the Activity lock. Missing or disabled records fail immediately; probe exceptions become unavailable. Healthy targets can continue while another target is being checked. If all remaining work consists of these offline rejections and their blocked dependents, the parent becomes partial with a reconnect explanation and no additional model decision. Active work and user-input continuations retain their own lifecycle.

An earlier claimed invocation follows receipt recovery, not this definitely-unstarted path. A currently offline host cannot establish that an earlier operation failed to execute.

Pairing a selected inbound Gateway

TLS pins identify the Gateway public key. Pairing identifies the controller allowed to send protected requests. First-use TLS capture and live-socket verification precede the application exchange below.

sequenceDiagram participant C as AuthenticatedOpener participant L as Controller pairing-cache lock participant G as Selected pinned Gateway participant P as Gateway pairing-state lock C->>L: Load retained controller key and exact peer receipt alt Matching controller receipt exists L-->>C: Reuse setup receipt else Pairing must be proved C->>G: GET pair challenge alt Gateway is unpaired G-->>C: Signed identity, nonce, timestamp and revision C->>C: Verify pinned Gateway proof and sign response C->>G: POST pairing response G->>P: Recheck unpaired state and matching revision alt This claimant wins P-->>G: Persist paired controller G-->>C: Signed acknowledgement C->>C: Verify acknowledgement else Another claimant already paired G-->>C: Conflict C->>G: Signed ownership status request G-->>C: Ownership proof or authentication rejection end else Gateway already paired C->>G: Signed ownership status request G-->>C: Ownership proof or authentication rejection end C->>L: Atomically cache only verified controller ownership end Note over C,G: Cached setup never removes per-request signature and replay checks

Pairing cannot replace another controller's established key. An initialized but missing or corrupt pairing record fails closed. The local reset changes pairing state while preserving the Gateway TLS identity. Reset commands and the broader connection-recovery workflow remain in the installation guide.

Signed HTTP admission and its retry boundary

sequenceDiagram participant C as Controller opener participant M as Gateway middleware participant A as Pairing and nonce authority participant O as Route and operation owner C->>C: Require selected origin and pairing opt Epoch-aware operation without a cached peer epoch C->>M: Signed runtime-purge status request M-->>C: Current epoch and purge state end C->>M: Signed method, exact target, body digest and epoch M->>M: Verify headers and initial runtime gate loop Until complete HTTP body M->>M: Receive, bound, hash and spool exact bytes end M->>M: Compare actual body digest M->>A: Recheck paired controller and consume nonce alt Authentication or admission fails before dispatch M-->>C: Classified rejection with no-execution proof where applicable opt Explicit rejected-v1 gateway_unpaired and retry unused C->>C: Remove cached pairing receipt and repeat setup once end else Authenticated body accepted A-->>M: Controller identity and pairing revision M->>M: Enter runtime admission and consume private policy envelope M->>O: Replay verified body under request context O-->>M: Result or stream with operation-owned outcome M-->>C: Response plus policy observations end Note over C,O: Ordinary HTTP errors or send failures never authorize automatic replay

Signatures bind the exact path and query ordering, method, identities, timestamp, nonce, body digest and optional epoch. The middleware rechecks pairing after hashing the upload, so reset during upload cannot admit the former controller. It then consumes private runtime-policy fields before forwarding the application body. The signed original bytes and this internal normalized body are different stages of the same authenticated request.

Public health and first-pairing routes have explicit exceptions. Protected WebSocket admission verifies an empty body and accepts replay state before the wrapped application handles the connection. HTTP body, time, pairing and replay bounds remain documented in transport identity and request authentication.

Only a recognized X-SMTO-Authentication: rejected-v1 response establishes the opener's authentication rejection boundary. It allows one automatic setup retry for gateway_unpaired; it does not retry other authentication failures or an operation's ordinary 401/403/409 response. Runtime-policy validation has its own pre-dispatch error response. Once dispatched, middleware propagates operation failures without inventing zero-execution facts. Response headers and complete SSE event boundaries carry policy observations separately from the business result.

Establishing the outbound control channel

Outbound Gateways initiate a WSS connection to an explicitly configured Server. They require WSS even on loopback and open no inbound listener for this mode.

sequenceDiagram participant G as Gateway connection owner participant T as Server TLS pin participant C as Controller connection route participant R as Configured registry and replay fences G->>T: Load pin or capture configured peer over TLS only G->>T: Verify actual connection certificate before WebSocket headers G->>C: Signed init with node, Gateway key, timestamp and nonce C->>R: Require configured node, pin identity and consume nonce C-->>G: Accept socket and send signed controller challenge G->>G: Verify challenge and retained controller identity G->>C: Signed capabilities bound to both nonces and identities opt Gateway has no paired controller G->>C: Include signed pairing challenge in capability hello end C->>C: Verify capability node and signature C-->>G: Auth acknowledgement with pairing material if needed G->>G: Complete first pairing if needed and recheck controller G->>C: Signed ready proof C->>R: Publish capabilities and register authenticated session C-->>G: hello_ack G->>G: Accept controller provenance and init nonce locally G->>G: Begin request receive loop

The controller consumes the initiation nonce before accepting the socket. A later failed handshake does not make that nonce reusable. It never creates a configured node from an arbitrary peer's name. Capability publication and session registration happen after the signed ready proof. A replacement session must retain the same verified Gateway identity; displaced waiters fail and the old socket is closed. An old disconnect cannot remove its replacement from the registry.

The mutual-proof receive steps have ten-second bounds. The Gateway's subsequent hello_ack receive has no separate wait_for deadline in this owner. The socket uses 20-second ping intervals/timeouts, a 16 MiB message bound and no proxy lookup. An identity-change block persists across reconnect attempts. Automatic reconnect backs off from one to thirty seconds with up to a quarter-second jitter; it establishes a connection without replaying earlier operations.

Sending an operation and observing its result

sequenceDiagram participant W as Controller worker participant S as Outbound session and event loop participant G as Gateway request task participant O as GatewayService provider W->>S: Request or stream with captured policy and accepted epoch S->>S: Allocate request ID and future or bounded event queue S->>S: Check authentication, runtime gate and socket under send lock S->>G: Correlated JSON request or binary transfer frame G->>G: Enter runtime admission and check epoch G->>G: Validate selected route and consume request policy G->>O: Dispatch through the shared service alt One-shot result O-->>G: Actual body or operation failure G-->>S: Correlated status, body and observations S-->>W: Resolve pending future once else Streaming command or terminal operation loop Synchronous iterator advanced in worker threads O-->>G: Operation event G-->>S: stream_event under send lock S-->>W: Queue event and policy observations end G-->>S: stream_end or stream_error S-->>W: End observation or raise peer error G->>O: Close iterator in finally end

The Gateway creates an independent task for each accepted request message. Tasks and to_thread workers inherit authenticated pairing provenance, including after socket loss. Sends are serialized per connection; providers retain their own operation/resource rules. The outbound path has an explicit dispatch table, so it does not expose every inbound FastAPI route automatically.

Binary messages are limited to framed transfer-chunk requests and corresponding pending responses. JSON cannot impersonate the binary chunk route. The controller ignores late or duplicate responses after a request finishes or times out; those frames cannot create new operations. Malformed binary requests close the Gateway socket, while malformed JSON request messages are skipped there. The controller route closes on its recognized protocol/parse failures.

Each stream queue holds 64 items, each limited to 256 KiB when serialized. Overflow discards that stream's queued observations and delivers an explicit 507 error. It does not block the shared socket, cancel the remote command or reconstruct lost output. Exiting the local generator removes its queue without sending remote cancellation. Gateway iterator cleanup is separate from provider-owned process termination; see terminal lifetimes.

Disconnect and recovery decisions

flowchart TD Failure[Request delivery or observation fails] --> Before{Known failure before sending?} Before -->|Yes| Rejected[Retain classified pre-execution failure] Before -->|No| Unknown[Preserve possible remote execution] Unknown --> Waiters[Fail local futures and streams on disconnect] Waiters --> Session[Reconnect and authenticate a new session] Unknown --> Owner[Consult owning job, invocation or transfer receipt] Owner --> Evidence{Exact result or reconciliation evidence?} Evidence -->|Yes| Project[Publish the established outcome] Evidence -->|No| Retain[Retain unknown outcome and recovery restrictions] Session --> Future[Allow newly authorized future requests] Rejected --> Future Retain --> Inspect[Inspect or use an explicitly supported recovery workflow]

Connection replacement releases local callers. It does not certify remote cancellation, process death or successful completion. Exact receipts and physical ownership evidence remain with jobs, Gateway state and transfer recovery. In particular, acknowledged copy bytes are a progress measurement. The transfer progress reducer can display a verification phase at 100% without completing the operation.

The outbound state lease spans reconnect delays, preventing local reset from racing a running owner. Its exit block closes the updater, browser/UI provider, transfer provider and artifact maintenance in order. It does not close every resource owned by the inbound application's lifespan. See the existing outbound lifecycle description for those distinctions.

Evidence and limits

Authentication tests exercise pairing races, retained identity, canonical signatures, replay, upload limits and rejection classification. Outbound fixtures check registry replacement and controller routing with in-memory peers. Admission tests use scripted models and injected health results to check deadlines, offline branches and recovery. Progress tests distinguish acknowledged bytes from operation completion. These checks do not certify native platform behavior or a production network. The existing TLS diagnostic limitation remains unchanged.
